## `snowflake` {#output-snowflake}

Inserts each batch into a Snowflake table through the SQL API, one statement for each batch. A batch that is larger than 8 MiB becomes more statements.

`columns` has the same format as on the `postgres` output. Each entry names a column, its type and the field to read. The default `field` is the name of the column. Without `columns`, the table has a `PAYLOAD` column of type `VARIANT` that contains each message.

Snowflake folds a name with no quotes to upper case, and so does this output. `table` and each column `name` go to upper case: `readings` is the table `READINGS`. A field name on the message does not change. Thus, a table that has a lower case name in quotes cannot be used.

Each statement uses the warehouse. Put a `buffer` on the input, so that statements are large and few. Snowflake does not enforce keys, so this output has none. A retry that follows a lost connection does not write the rows two times.

The output creates the table if it does not exist. Set `create_table` to false for a table that another system owns. The output does not change an existing table.

| field | type | | description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `connection` | `snowflake` connection | <Badge type="warning" text="required" /> | The name of the snowflake connection to insert through. Declare the connection in the connections file. The connection gives the account, the warehouse, the database and the schema. |
| `table` | `string` | <Badge type="warning" text="required" /> | The table to insert into. The output creates it if it does not exist. You can add a schema (`staging.readings`). This schema replaces the schema of the connection. Use only letters, digits and underscores. |
| `columns` | `list of column` | <Badge type="info" text="optional" /> | The column for each message field. If you do not set it, the output keeps each full message in a `PAYLOAD` column of type `VARIANT`. |
| `create_table` | `boolean` | <Badge type="info" text="optional" /> | Create the table on start if it does not exist. The default is true. |
| `on_extra_fields` | `ignore` \| `error` | <Badge type="info" text="optional" /> | What to do with a message that has fields that no column reads. |

**`columns` — each entry**

| field | type | | description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `string` | <Badge type="warning" text="required" /> | The name of the column in the table. Use only letters, digits and underscores. |
| `type` | `text` \| `integer` \| `bigint` \| `float` \| `decimal` \| `boolean` \| `timestamp` \| `date` \| `uuid` \| `json` | <Badge type="warning" text="required" /> | The type of the column. The output checks each value against it. |
| `field` | `string` | <Badge type="info" text="optional" /> | The field to read, as a dotted path. The default is the name of the column. |
| `message` | `boolean` | <Badge type="info" text="optional" /> | Write the full message to this column. Use it only with a `json` column. Do not use it with `field`. |
| `nullable` | `boolean` | <Badge type="info" text="optional" /> | Whether the column accepts `NULL`. The default is true. With `false`, the output makes the column `NOT NULL`, and a missing field is an error. |
| `on_missing` | `null` \| `error` \| `skip_row` | <Badge type="info" text="optional" /> | What to do with a message that does not have the field. The default is `null`, or `error` for a column that is not nullable. |
